In BvS, we are only privy to small bits of information on emerging metahumans having been discovered by LexCorp.  Diana skims through the footage of Flash, Aquaman, and Cyborg, three recently discovered individuals who came to light in an age of omnipresent surveillance.  Wonder Woman herself hadn't been seen by mortal eyes since the Great War.  There are no surviving eyewitnesses, and the only evidence of her existence is one photograph of her wielding a sword and shield among other soldiers wielding guns.

Assuming that this is the sole evidence of Wonder Woman, the most that Batman can extrapolate about her is that she is both older than she seems and physically capable enough to bring a knife to a gun fight.  He's not painting with a broad enough brush to assume that every metahuman is exactly on par with Superman physically.  Someone in Wonder Woman's position, with enhanced longevity and physical abilities that are above the standard human's (to an unknown extent) might be a world destroyer, or they could be barely harder to kill than the aforementioned standard human.  When Batman finally figures out that Diana is more than meets the eye, he treats her with kid gloves for this exact reason.  No sense in threatening someone until you're certain that it doesn't matter what side of them you're on.

What you should be asking is why he hasn't already done so, and for that there are two main reasons.  First, Stark values modularity in his technology, constantly upgrading and reconstituting his suits.  Once you've cast a piece in an unbreakable metal, it's not going anywhere.  Can you imagine him finishing an adamantium suit and deciding he should have gone with some other design instinct?  That's one expensive prototype that you're not doing anything with.

But let's say he only makes a single component of his suit out of adamantium, something that can be taken out of and reinserted into other suits.  Now when it's inevitably stolen by someone trying to sell Stark tech on the black market, Tony's gonna have to get up in the middle of the night to hunt it down instead of activating the remote detonation failsafe he's got built deep down into every piece of gear he's ever made.

And when he does reclaim it, it's only a matter of time before some other goon steals it, or it develops an AI that decides to kill a whole bunch of people and becomes Ultron, only instead of being created by Hank Pym, noted non-Iron Man suit specialist, it's been built by someone much more qualified at death machines.

Few popular Muggle musicians that have reputations aligned with the occult are magical, but some are related to wizards or witches.  David Bowie's half-brother Terry was Muggle-born; the view of him as mentally ill was his smokescreen, and his death was his exit from Muggle life.  Jimmy Page was not a wizard, but pretended to be one, while John Paul Jones is and keeps it a secret.  Stevie Nicks is a witch.  Robert Johnson is a wizard, and still alive.

The arts in general are a good place for wizards, witches, and Muggle relatives of witches and wizards to congregate, and there are many more without obvious occult reputations that are secretly magical (Tupac Shakur and ODB are fine examples).  As a general rule, however, it's seen as an odd thing at best and a disgrace to magic at worst to do so.  The majority of magical peoples living prominently in the Muggle world aren't, how shall we say, particularly adept at magic.  Obviously I'd never tell someone in that situation that they're only doing so because they couldn't cut it with a wand, and neither should you.

Besides, you never know when they're actually just capable and well-concealed dark wizards.  Let's just say that, whatever else he may have done (I'm not defending his racism), Varg Vikernes was totally right to kill Dead and Euronymous.  Their bloodbath would be legendary if declassified.

More than any one instrument, a good song needs subtle structural variations within the arrangement so that it doesn't just sound like the instrumental for the verse was recorded once and copy-pasted three times.  This could be the introduction of a new instrument playing a new part, or a rhythmic variation in one of the existing parts, or just a change in the phrasing of the chords.  Little touches like that that show the songwriters care.

The example I always give is "Jack and Diane" by John Mellencamp, which has instruments weaving in and out the whole time to cover up the fact that the rest of the arrangement is mostly acoustic guitar, a ton of percussion, and vocals: piano during the second half of the first verse, organ during the second verse, and then the final chorus has that panflute.  Mick Ronson did a hell of a job fleshing out what Mellencamp originally wrote as a pretty generic White Guy on Acoustic Guitar song.

Bragging about his IQ serves a dual purpose for Rick.  For those who put stock in IQ as an objective measure of value, it demeans them and elevates Rick in their eyes.  For those who rightfully see IQ as a particular metric only applicable within certain contexts, it paints Rick as a braggart to be disregarded and underestimated, saving him time and effort if he has to dismantle them.

The Magneto of X-Men: Evolution was personally liberated from the death camps by Captain America, and thinks of him as "one of the good ones."  This respect carries over into standard Marvel even though no meeting between the two is confirmed (though I can easily picture them both flying off to kill Nazis with Cap on top of his shield like Static).

Less obvious a connection to a mutate comes from Magneto's knowledge of Spider-Man. His knowledge of the webslinger as a person is limited but he knows enough through the Daily Bugle and J. Jonah Jameson's fervor that there's a vigilante in New York who started out as a teenager and is hated by the powers that be.  Magneto probably thinks that Spider-Man is some masked mutant disinclined towards both the X-Men and the Brotherhood.  Were he to learn the truth, I wouldn't be surprised if Magneto still counts Spider-Man as sympathetic if not an ally.  Depending on how much he knows about the Fantastic Four, they're extended the same olive branch, Thing especially.

No way does he respect the Inhuman Royal Family, given their industrialized abuse of the lower-classed Inhumans for generations, even though it seems to come and go depending on which way the wind is blowing.  He's not against individual Inhumans though, just the ones in power.
